Senses.Explanation: Literally, “not hanging a single thread”: not wearing even one strand of clothing. The late Chan records deploy nakedness as a description of a person after successive stripping: Xueguan compares it to taking off clothes and undoing a belt, layer after layer, then asks what could still be removed from “a fellow not wearing a single thread” (一絲不掛的漢子). Other records pair the phrase with “coming and going freely” (來去自如) or with “the myriad forms all manifest” (萬象齊彰). The Zen bend is therefore directly visible in its use as an appraisal of a person rather than only a state of undress. The records do not define an inner state behind the image, and this entry does not supply one.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase occurs 10 times in 9 allowlisted texts. The witnesses are concentrated in seventeenth-century records, so the sense is multi-text but late. Searches found the clothing comparison, person-appraisal, paired predicates, and no morphological variant or independent formula that establishes another sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 忽有箇一絲不掛的漢子出來，還教伊脫箇甚麼？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 雪關禪師語錄, instruction on relinquishing what is prized. Xueguan Zhiyin is the exact speaker: after comparing the process to stripping off clothing layer by layer, he asks what could still be removed from a person with not one thread attached.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一絲不掛來去自如？仰望洪慈，策其末路。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 費隱禪師語錄, Reply to Grand Historian Cao Exue, personal name Cao Xun (復太史曹峨雪居士諱勳). Cao Xun is the exact writer of the stored incoming words, introduced by Feiyin Tongrong as 來諭; Feiyin's response begins only after that quoted appeal.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一絲不掛，萬象齊彰。性相融通，自它俱利。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 紫竹林顓愚衡和尚語錄, instruction on the monastic robe. Zhuanyu Guanheng is the exact author: after describing the robe's transmission and dimensions, he says that with not one thread attached the myriad forms all manifest and nature and marks interpenetrate.

Occurrences.Kwic: 不惟善能解脫塵勞一絲不掛，且爾直入無上菩提如箭射鵠、如刀破竹
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 雪關禪師語錄, Xueguan Zhiyin's prose instruction for a layman named Shi. Xueguan Zhiyin is the exact author: he says that equal regard toward good and bad circumstances not only frees one from dusty toil with not one thread attached but also permits direct entry into unsurpassed awakening.
